newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine current account deficit seen widening.
newsitem.headline: Philippine current account deficit seen widening.

text.p: The Philippines' merchandise trade deficit narrowed in the first half of the year but it might not be enough to prevent the current account from going further into the red, analysts said on Tuesday.
The National Statistics Office said the trade gap narrowed to $5.63 billion in the first six months from $6.05 billion a year earlier. Exports grew 22 percent while imports increased by 11 percent.
"The trade deficit is still okay. But I would rather focus on the current account deficit. Services are negative. That's not good," said Peregrine Securities economist Luz Lorenzo.
On Monday, the central bank said the current account deficit widened to $2.02 billion in the first four months of the year from $1.47 billion in the year-earlier period.

The central bank data showed non-merchandise trade, or the services account, posted a deficit of $100 million in April, pulling the surplus for January-April down to $1.45 billion versus $2.32 billion last year.

"It looks like there's pressure for the current account deficit to worsen," said Joven Babaan, research director of SBC Warburg, adding that he had expected the current account gap to widen to only $4.5 billion this year.
"As early as March, there appears to be speculation of a possible depreciation given the fact foreign currency deposit conversions (into pesos) have gone down," he said.

He cited the central bank data showing that peso conversions of foreign currency deposits dwindled to $201 million in March and $164 million in April from an average of $500 million each in the first two months.

It was in April when Thailand's financial woes started to spill over to the Philippines' financial markets, sending the equities market to a two-year low and forcing an effective devaluation of the peso on July 11.
The peso fell to a new low of 30.24 to dollar on Monday, a drop of about 14 percent since the de facto devaluation.
But Babaan said the peso's depreciation would eventually lead to stronger exports and higher income from overseas workers and tourism receipts.
Peregrine's Lorenzo said the depreciation would lead her to forecast a wider trade deficit this year from her earlier estimate of $13.3 billion.
"Probably a little higher," she said. "At once, you have to pay for higher cost of goods but your higher export orders will not come until later."
